evidence_quotes.quote: Here, we assessed health risks from consumption of contaminated well water on the Crow Reservation by conducting a community-engaged, cumulative risk assessment. Well water testing, surveys and interviews were used to collect data on contaminant concentrations, water treatment methods, well water consumption, and well and septic system protection and maintenance practices.
The national scope of the health risk from consuming this water has not been assessed as home wells are largely unregulated and data on well water treatment and consumption are lacking.
Neither the Tribe nor county conducts public education on how to maintain and protect wells and septic systems, nor what the health risks could be from contaminated well water.
One hundred ninety-seven people from 165 Tribal families completed surveys and 164 wells were tested.
Another 20% (about 220 families, 970 people) have such unpalatable well water that they haul all water for drinking and cooking.

criterion_notes.c1: Borderline/unclear: the study investigates self-supplied private domestic wells (in homes that already have indoor plumbing) and primarily conducts an environmental health water-quality and cumulative contaminant exposure assessment rather than examining utility or community water/sanitation service access, although it does report descriptive household coping with unpalatable well water via hauling water, purchasing bottled water, and cost barriers to home treatment.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails under BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor: references to federal non-regulation of private wells, non-applicability of state well-testing laws on reservation trust lands, and secondary citations in the Discussion to limited environmental enforcement and jurisdictional complexity serve solely as unanalysed background context, while EPA MCLs/SMCLs/RfDs are used strictly as toxicological risk benchmarks. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, no rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or regulatory structure) is empirically analysed, and unanalysed macro-governance background is explicitly out of scope.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes: primary empirical mixed-methods CBPR study combining laboratory chemical/microbial testing of 164 home wells, surveys of 197 individuals from 165 Crow Tribal families, 30 in-depth key-informant interviews, and secondary analysis of ~650 Indian Health Service well records.
criterion_notes.c4: Borderline/unclear: the primary outcomes are water-quality benchmark exceedances (Risk Quotients), cumulative non-carcinogenic Hazard Indices, carcinogenic risk estimates, and household well-water ingestion/treatment practices, though it also reports descriptive rates of well-water avoidance (20% neither drinking nor cooking with well water and hauling/purchasing alternative water) and affordability barriers to bottled water and treatment equipment.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes: population and units of analysis (home wells and rural Crow Tribal households/adults), exposures (inorganic well-water contaminant concentrations and consumption rates), outcomes (Hazard Index, carcinogenic risk, MCL/SMCL exceedances, and household water use/coping), and cross-sectional CBPR mixed-methods / cumulative risk assessment design are clearly reported.

study_design: Community-based participatory cross-sectional mixed-methods study and deterministic cumulative health risk assessment (well water laboratory testing, household surveys, key-informant interviews, and secondary well-drilling records)
population_and_sample: Rural Crow (Apsaalooke) Tribal families using private home wells on the Crow Reservation, Montana (units of analysis: home well and household/adult respondent; n = 164 wells tested, 197 adults from 165 families surveyed, 30 key informants interviewed, plus ~650 historical Indian Health Service well records)
exposure: Inorganic contaminants in private home well water (uranium, manganese, nitrate + nitrite as N, arsenic, zinc, total dissolved solids, sulfate, iron, hardness, and pH) and household well-water consumption practices
outcome: Cumulative non-carcinogenic health risk (Hazard Quotients and Hazard Index > 1.0), carcinogenic risk from arsenic and uranium, EPA primary/secondary drinking water standard exceedances (Risk Quotients), household well-water consumption vs. avoidance (hauling water or buying bottled water), and use of home water treatment technologies
rationale: Excluded (E03 - Wrong exposure, and water-quality risk assessment without governance analysis per Exclusion Criterion 3). This community-engaged environmental health study assesses inorganic chemical contamination (U, Mn, NO3-, As, Zn, TDS, Fe) in private home wells on the Crow Reservation, calculating cumulative toxicological Hazard Indices and cancer risk alongside household water consumption, treatment, and coping behaviors. Although the paper notes in background and discussion sections that private home wells are unregulated federally, state laws do not apply on reservation trust lands, and prior literature cites limited environmental enforcement, it collects and analyses no empirical data on any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor under either the plain wording or the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2.
